chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
title: Leaving Ella's band after the Holyoke meeting
summary: At a meeting with Gale, Ella and Eddie Barefield, McRae walked out over the unsigned agreement and left that night, without bitterness.

bands.name: Ella Fitzgerald and Her Famous Orchestra

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: BEGINNING OF TAPE 5

After we finished the Apollo Theater, Moe Gale come up -- Remember, this was not a bitter thing. We had no bitterness, you know. This is business. Everything has always been business with me. We disagree, we don't disagree, so I don't hate you for it. You don't (inaudible), you know, this is a matter of business, you know. So, he told me he would see me in Baltimore. So the first week went by -- He didn't come up for the opening. He didn't know -- we made good up there -- he didn't come up for the opening at all. The third week we were there, the fourth week we were there, he came up the last day of the closing. It was on a Saturday night. And he had booked at Holyoke, Mass. a date with -- I think one of the bands that supposed to be up there was -- Supposed to be two bands on that date, the next Sunday. See, I'm trying to think. One of
the bands is out of New York. A white band out of New York.
It might've been Woody Herman. I know it was an outstanding band. Somebody like Woody Herman, or something like that.
And Ella and the band -- Chick Webb's band. We were supposed to play a show together. First, he would open the show and we would close the show with our act, you know.
So that night at the hotel where we playing, Moe Gale comes in after the second show. And he had with him my friend, Eddie Barefield.
So after we came off the stand we talked and everything. I greeted (inaudible). All the guys were glad to see Eddie Barefield and everything like that.
And we had a meeting with Ella and Moe Gale -- had called a meeting -- and myself to talk over some business.
He told us, 'Look, you're playing Holyoke, Mass. tomorrow,' and everything, so and so and so.

I say, 'How about my agreement? You bring the agreement along? You work it out?' (inaudible) you know.
And I went over the agreement with him and told him what I wanted. And Ella and him couldn't come to an agreement on it, so I walked out.
So I say, 'I think you better go in there and talk to Moe, Eddie Barefield, because he brought you up -- if I wasn't going to agree to his terms, I was going to leave the band.'
He think I was going to leave, because Moe knew me real well. When I say I'm going to do something, I'm going to do it.
And then if we come to that, we couldn't get along, forget it.
So Barefield came out and say, 'What're you going to do? You going to leave the band?'

I say, 'Well, he didn't bring my agreement. I'm just at the end of the road with him. He understood that when I came here. I told him that (inaudible) there in his Cadillac in the back of the Apollo Theater.'

I say, "Now, we just finished the last show. I'll see you in Boston, right?" "Well, we agreed on (inaudible)?" "Yeah." "See all the write-ups in the paper?" "Yeah." Band is success all the way back -- all to the coast and back. We broke record after record. People just lined the streets.
When we played St. Louis, people brought their kids in the ballroom, the little girls, (inaudible) the ticket.

We were getting like -- first, when we went out there with Chick Webb, Chick was giving them like a hundred dollars was going to be given away. A hundred and fifty dollars. Seventy-five dollars or fifty dollars for, you know, first little girl, you know. Seventy-five -- right on down the line.
There was a hundred dollars he give away, you know. They had these little girls singing A Tisket A Tasket. Whoever won the first prize
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
(inaudible), the second prize. Chick would pay out of his pocket, you know, 'A Tisket A Tasket' prize, you know.
So that continued after Chick had passed. We continued doing that.
So when we came back -- So Barefield took over the band.
Barefield asked me-- he say, "Do me a favor. Will you go to Holyoke, Mass. do that show and then I'll take the band over."
I say, "No, I can't do that."
"I tell you what I'm going to do for you the show that you're going to do tomorrow. The last show that I'm going to do up here tonight. That's going to be the show."
"Everything Ella is going to sing on the stage tomorrow, we'll do in the show. One of the band is going to play the opening number, but we're going to close it."
"That'll be your show tomorrow, whatever you want to do -- what Taft gonna do (inaudible). I wrote it all down. It's all written down for you."

"(Inaudible) you got to do, you know. Good musicians, you know. Go on out there and just bring (inaudible). The band play the drop of a dime. Don't worry about it." I went and made my
So that night, 12:05, (inaudible) come back to New York. That was the end of it with Ella.
And it was a very good trip. I mean, it was a very good time. Wasn't no bitterness. We didn't end on bitter note. Just that it was an agreement that we had, you know.
And I figured that I had did everything that I could do, you know.
